outcome: One build and release path lets an application move between the data centre and cloud without a rewrite.
overview: Banks in the Gulf run applications in their own data centres and in cloud, and the two estates drift apart — different build pipelines, different runtimes, different operational habits — until moving a workload becomes a project rather than a decision. Red Hat OpenShift puts one Kubernetes platform on both sides of that line, so an application built once runs in either place under the same policies and the same release process. The value is optionality: regulated workloads stay where the regulator expects them while everything else moves on its own merits. Redington scopes the platform against a named first wave of applications and measures release lead time against the pre-build baseline.

benefits.text: One build and release path for applications whether they land on-premises or in cloud
benefits.limits: Holds for applications that are already containerised or can be; a mainframe or a licensed appliance workload does not become portable because the platform is

benefits.text: Placement becomes a residency and cost decision rather than a re-platforming project
benefits.limits: Data gravity and integration with fixed on-premises systems still constrain placement; the platform removes the runtime obstacle, not the data one

benefits.text: A single operational model to staff and to audit, instead of two
benefits.limits: Subscription-model claim: the benefit depends on the customer consolidating onto the subscription rather than running it alongside what it was meant to replace

residency: Runs entirely inside the customer estate; the control plane can sit in-country on customer hardware or in a local cloud region, so regulated workloads never leave the jurisdiction

notFor.situation: An estate that has already standardised on another managed Kubernetes service
notFor.why: A second Kubernetes distribution doubles the platform team’s surface without adding a capability the first one lacks

notFor.situation: An application portfolio that is predominantly packaged, licensed software
notFor.why: A container platform improves the delivery path for software you build; it does nothing for software you buy and cannot repackage

scope:
Model: Redington solutions engineering with an accredited Red Hat implementation partner · Duration: 10–14 weeks to first-wave production, depending on how many applications are in the wave
Support model: Vendor subscription support for the platform; Redington coordinates the vendor case and holds the delivery relationship. Optional managed platform operations with an agreed response target.
1) Assessment — application portfolio review, candidacy scoring and first-wave selection
2) Design — cluster sizing, network and storage integration, policy baseline and the promotion path
3) Build — clusters in both locations, registry, pipelines and policy under change control
4) Migrate and hand over — first-wave applications live, runbooks written, platform team shadowed
deliverables: An application image built once deploys unmodified to both clusters and passes the same policy checks
The promotion path from build to production runs without a manual step outside change approval
The customer platform team completes a documented upgrade on the non-production cluster unaided
effort: 10–14 weeks to first-wave production, depending on how many applications are in the wave
languages: English delivery; Arabic executive materials on request
